https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: 1:02 Anti-migrant rally and counter-protesters face off in Portsmouth – video Far right Portsmouth experiences second weekend of anti-immigration protests Rightwing activists faced a heavy police presence and counter-demonstrations to their march against small boat crossings Sammy Gecsoyler and Raphael Boyd Sat 12 Sep 2026 13.41 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 15.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two men and a teenage boy have been arrested in Portsmouth at a far-right protest against immigration. Far-right activists have gathered in Portsmouth for a second weekend after a small boat with 140 people seeking asylum on board was intercepted last Sunday while heading towards the city. They were greeted by counter-protesters as police warned they would not tolerate incitement of fear or violence. From black-clad agitators to an appeal for ‘Tommo’s Mum’: an unsettling week with the Patriot Platform Read more One of the arrested, a 76-year-old man from Southampton, was detained on suspicion of concealing his identity at the Portsmouth protest. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary had warned that protesters wearing face coverings could be arrested under powers in the Crime and Policing Act. A 33-year-old man from Portsmouth was also arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway and a 16-year-old boy, also from Portsmouth, was arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in relation to scenes last Sunday. View image in fullscreen Protesters gather for a counter-demonstration in Portsmouth on Saturday. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock Donna Jones, the police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that they “thankfully didn’t see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people’s property” and that “with the exception of a few people, it was peaceful and conducted in accordance with the new law calling for their faces to be uncovered”. Jones added: “The people of Portsmouth deserve to go about their business without fear and disruption. “While some may think it was arbitrary to use the new power directing people to remove face coverings, the police ensured it was implemented equally and impartially for everyone involved. “I will ensure this power is used proportionately in the future for both sides of the spectrum of protesters.” View image in fullscreen Demonstrators at an anti-immigration march in Portsmouth on Saturday. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA In Portsmouth city centre, there was a large police presence where demonstrators assembled to march on Saturday. Some protesters held union flags while some wearing Portsmouth patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road. A man with a megaphone got the crowd chanting “stop the boats”. He said the protest was against “illegal men invading the shores”. In the neighbouring car park, demonstrators holding Stand Up to Racism (SUTR) and Refugees Welcome banners gathered. Signs included: “RNLI are heroes, no one is illegal” and “stop pretending your racism is patriotism”. Hundreds of people also gathered in Glasgow for an anti-immigration rally and associated counter-protest. View image in fullscreen The Pink Ladies event in Glasgow. The event passed off peacefully amid a heavy police presence and segregation of opposing protesters. Photograph: Iain Masterton/Alamy Live News The Pink Ladies movement organised their event at Glasgow Green, prompting opposing groups, including SUTR, to arrange a counter-protest. The two groups were contained in separate areas on the eastern side of the park, with the People’s Palace and a heavy police presence between them. Ch Supt Stevie Dolan warned of a “strong response” if there was any violence after flashpoints at a previous protest in the same park in July. MSPs Alison Thewliss, a Scottish government minister, and Iris Duane were at the SUTR rally, with the Scottish Trades Union Congress general secretary Roz Foyer. View image in fullscreen Police officers contain counter-protesters against a Pink Ladies rally beside Glasgow’s People’s Palace. Photograph: Steve Welsh/PA Prominent figures on the Scottish right, such as Reform UK’s deputy leader in Scotland, Thomas Kerr, and the Reform councillor Audrey Dempsey, attended the Pink Ladies event. Saturday’s protests came after hundreds of far-right activists descended on Portsmouth last Sunday after a small boat crossing the Channel approached the city. The demonstrators tried to stop those onboard from being processed. Hampshire police said: “We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.” The opposing groups were allocated specific locations at which they could gather under protest conditions. Failure to comply with conditions could lead to arrest, police said. The anti-immigration protest marched to Guildhall Square and the counter-protest followed later on the same route. View image in fullscreen Lifejackets at Eastney abandoned by people seeking asylum who made the crossing from France on 6 September. Photograph: Ollie Thompson/Solent News & Photo Agency/Solent News The incident with the small boat last Sunday was thought to be the first time such a large vessel containing asylum seekers had been brought to Portsmouth and the first time that a significant group of anti-migrant protesters had tried to block newly arrived asylum seekers from being processed. Small boat crossings have fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year. While the Home Office has disrupted the smugglers’ business model , their methods appear to have evolved by launching boats – such as the one that arrived last Sunday – from different parts of the French coast much farther from the UK, making the crossings more dangerous. Most small boat arrivals are rescued by Border Force and RNLI vessels on the English side of the Channel and brought ashore at Dover. RNLI volunteers and staff have faced abuse from protesters over their rescue work bringing some small boat migrants ashore. The first man charged over last weekend’s anti-migrant demonstration in Portsmouth appeared in court on Saturday. View image in fullscreen Police officers at Eastney beach, Portsmouth, where hundreds of protesters gathered to meet a small boat arriving from France. Photograph: PA Del Leon Somerville, 42, of Paulsgrove in Portsmouth, appeared before the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable in the execution of their duty. Assistant chief constable Tony Rowlinson said Somerville’s arrest was the “first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests” and hoped it would send a “clear warning” to those planning future disruption and disorder. The government condemned what it described as the “thuggish behaviour” of the protesters last Sunday. “We condemn the intimidating and thuggish behaviour we are seeing tonight,” a government spokesperson said. “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder.” Number of UK anti-migrant vigilante groups surges in last 18 months Read more The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, met police on Thursday for reassurance they are ready to move quickly in dealing with “far-right groups” seeking to intimidate communities after last weekend’s events in Dover and Portsmouth. Official vehicles were damaged in Portsmouth and a small number of officers were injured , police said. In Dover, crowds of masked men blocked road access to the port in scenes that were condemned by politicians of all parties. Mahmood said: “These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents. “This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons.” Explore more on these topics Far right Portsmouth Protest Immigration and asylum Refugees Glasgow news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid home where she had lived for more than seven decades led to protests. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters View image in fullscreen The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid home where she had lived for more than seven decades led to protests. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters Spain Eviction of 87-year-old puts Spain’s deepening housing crisis in the spotlight Images of Maricarmen Abascal being forcibly removed from her home sparked protests and a reckoning over the country’s soaring real estate market Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Sun 27 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 27 Sep 2026 00.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Images of an octogenarian being evicted from the home she had lived in for seven decades on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police officers, sparked indignation across Spain . Hours later, people began taking to the streets. In Madrid, an estimated 10,000 people turned up on Wednesday, wielding signs that read “Shame” and “Out with the vulture funds”, to protest against the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal. From the northern tip of Spain to the south, people poured into plazas calling for a nationwide reckoning over access to housing. Police use teargas on protesters as disabled woman, 87, evicted from Madrid home Read more The catalyst was the eviction of Abascal, now known across the country by her first name, Maricarmen. The 87-year-old woman with a disability said she had been forced to leave her home after she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment. “This eviction is the canary in the coalmine,” said political scientist Cristina Monge. “It’s become a symbol, seen as the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the issue of housing.” It was, as newspaper El País said in an editorial, a glimpse of a housing market that had become completely unmoored from the average income in Spain, as rents rose 80% in a decade, while the cost of homes had climbed by 63%. “The law was upheld, and the market worked. But it is the law of the jungle in a broken market, and it is a failure.” The investment fund linked to the eviction of Maricarmen did not reply to a request for comment from the Guardian. Saturday saw around 25,000 people, according to government figures, take to the streets of Madrid, rattling keys as they called for measures to curb rising housing costs and make evictions more difficult. Some brought tents and sleeping bags, announcing plans to set up a protest camp in Madrid’s central Sol plaza. The eviction had left many in Spain grappling with a sense of “powerlessness”, said Monge, given that the issue of housing had also been at the forefront of the Spanish Indignados movement, or 15-M, the years-long anti-austerity and anti-corruption protest movement that involved millions of Spaniards and reshaped the country’s politics. “Now, 15 years later, housing is still the number one concern of Spaniards. And there are still evictions every day, to the order of about 25,000 per year,” she said. “But the paradox is that the country’s government includes some of the same people who led the 15-M protests. And still, housing remains an enormous challenge.” View image in fullscreen Rents and house prices have soared in the last decade in Spain. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters As anger mounted this week, politicians laid the blame on each other for the eviction. Rights campaigners and researchers weighed in with potential solutions, citing the more than 3m homes believed to be sitting empty across the country or government figures that suggest social housing makes up just 2.5% of the total stock in Spain, compared to 14% in France and 34% in the Netherlands. The head of one of the country’s biggest labour unions called for investment funds to be “kicked out” of the housing market. “Homes are for living in, not for large corporations to do business,” said Unai Sordo of the Workers’ Commissions (CCOO) as he called for a tax system that would make “the business of hoarding homes unprofitable”. The UN’s special rapporteur on the right to housing, Koldo Casla, called on Spain to amend the laws governing its legal system, describing it as “impossible to understand” how the profitability of a real estate company had been prioritised over Maricarmen’s right to housing. The leftwing coalition Sumar, the junior partner in the government, said it would push the socialist-led government to greenlight the expropriation of Maricarmen’s former home as well as put forward a package of rent freezes. The widespread demand for change has cast a spotlight on the deep divisions that exist among Spain’s political parties when it comes to the issue of housing. These divisions were laid bare earlier this year when the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the hardline Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted to end a moratorium on evictions that for six years had managed to shield some vulnerable tenants from eviction. On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who is under fire for not doing more to ensure his government had carried through on its promises of making housing a priority, promised to swiftly introduce a raft of measures. “Maricarmen’s eviction is a social tragedy that we cannot accept,” he said. While his government had in 2023 managed to pass legislation that strengthened tenant protection and widened access to rent control, regions led by the People’s party had wielded their powers over housing to avoid implementing parts of the legislation. Among those who had ignored parts of the legislation was the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, who in recent weeks has faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office. The striking contrast between the allegations against Ayuso and the eviction of Maricarmen has repeatedly cropped up this week, from the decision to hold Wednesday’s protest in Madrid on a boulevard next to the penthouse, to the chants urging “Ayuso’s penthouse for Maricarmen”. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators gather in front of a penthouse bought as an office with public funds by Isabel Díaz Ayuso. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images The regional leader has so far sought to downplay the significance of Maricarmen’s eviction, describing it as “one out of the 25,500 that take place every year in Spain” and noting that it had been authorised by the country’s courts. While the story of Maricarmen had dominated headlines, turning the octogenarian into the poster woman for those bearing the brunt of Spain’s soaring real estate market, many pointed to her plight as a glimpse of a wider reality. “Maricarmen’s case is not an isolated incident; it is just one more example of the suffering endured by thousands of households in Spain,” Amnesty International Spain said in a statement. “Bold measures must be taken immediately. Institutions must go beyond simply expressing regret in the press, they must take action.” Explore more on these topics Spain Europe Renting property Housing Social housing Protest features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/29/eld.text: Menü Kereső Eldőlt, hogy mégsem épül kínai elektrolitgyár Szolnokon Gazdaság Pál Tamás Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Nem épít Szolnokon elektrolitgyárat a kínai KunlunChem – jelentette be kedd este a vállalat a Facebook-oldalán. Bejegyzésükben azt írták, hogy tiszteletben tartják Szolnok és a helyi közösség akaratát, ezért úgy döntöttek, nem folytatják tovább a beruházásuk megvalósítását a városban. Szolnok polgármestere, Györfi Mihály úgy reagált a hírre, hogy ezzel egész Szolnok győzött. „Elértük, amiért harcoltunk! A KunlunChem bejelentette, hogy nem építik meg a Szolnok határába tervezett elektrolitgyárat. Ezzel véget ért az a fideszes mutyi, amit évekig készítettek elő titokban Orbán emberei, köztük Szalay Ferenccel és társaival” – írta Facebook-oldalán a polgármester. A szolnoki közgyűlés már április végén úgy döntött, hogy nem támogatják az elektrolitgyár megépítését . Az akkori ülésen a testület visszavonta azt a fideszes többség által még 2024-ben hozott döntést, amivel elvi támogatást nyújtottak az akkumulátoripari beruházásokhoz. Györfi a támogatás visszavonását azzal indokolta, hogy a beruházó részéről nem történt érdemi előrelépés a létesítménnyel kapcsolatos tájékoztatásban, és állítása szerint a projekt tényleges környezetterhelési paraméterei sem voltak ismertek, például a valós kibocsátási adatok, a veszélyes anyagok kezelése vagy a szállítási útvonalak. Emellett a lakosság is aggódott a veszélyes anyagokkal kapcsolatos kockázatok miatt. Júliusban Rost Andrea, a térség tiszás országgyűlési képviselője bejelentette, hogy nemzetgazdasági szempontból már nem minősül kiemelt beruházásnak a Szolnok és Abony közé tervezett elektrolitgyár. Szijjártó Péter akkori külügyminiszter még 2025 márciusában jelentette be, hogy Szolnokon építi fel az első európai üzemét a KunlunChem kínai elektrolitgyártó cég. KunlunChem a világ öt legnagyobb elektrolitgyártója közé tartozik, és a tervek szerint a BMW és a Mercedes elektromos autóinak beszállítója lett volna. A korábbi tervek szerint a negyvenmilliárd forintos beruházás százhúsz új munkahelyet teremtett volna. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak!
